content: 1. Juniperus communis (juniper) has specific dosing recommendations based on its indications. For example, the manufacturer’s instructions may suggest 800 mg orally twice daily (PO BID), or 1-2 grams of berries orally three times daily (PO TID). Alternatively, one cup of tea made by steeping 1 teaspoon of crushed berries (2-3 grams) in 150 mL of boiling water for 10 minutes can be consumed orally three times daily. A liquid preparation of 2 mL can also be taken orally three times daily. 2. Juniper is used for various conditions, including dyspepsia, flatulence, heartburn, bloating, loss of appetite, urinary tract infections (UTIs), kidney and bladder stones, snakebites, intestinal worms, gastrointestinal infections, diabetes, and cancer. Topically, it is applied for rheumatic pains, inflammatory diseases, and wounds. 3. There is insufficient reliable information regarding the effectiveness of juniper for these indications. However, it is known to possess diuretic properties. 4. Juniper may interact with diuretic medications such as amiloride, bendroflumethiazide, bumetanide, chlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, cyclopenthiazide, drospirenone, ethacrynic acid, furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide, methyclothiazide, metolazone, spironolactone, torsemide, and triamterene. It may either potentiate or interfere with diuretic therapy. While juniper has diuretic effects, high doses may cause kidney damage. Caution and close monitoring are advised when combining juniper with these medications. 5. Juniper may also interact with antidiabetic medications, including acarbose, glimepiride, glipizide, glyburide, insulin aspart, insulin detemir, insulin glargine, insulin glulisine, insulin lispro, insulin NPH, regular human insulin, metformin, miglitol, nateglinide, pioglitazone, repaglinide, rosiglitazone, saxagliptin, sitagliptin, and vildagliptin. These interactions are thought to occur via pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially increasing the risk of hypoglycemia. Although the significance of these interactions is unknown, they are considered theoretical and require close monitoring. 6. During pregnancy, juniper should be avoided as it may cause uterine contractions and kidney inflammation. It is categorized as unsafe for use during pregnancy. There is no available information regarding its safety during lactation. 7. In general, juniper is considered acceptable for use in non-pregnant individuals, as controlled studies in pregnant women have not shown evidence of fetal risk. However, its use should be approached with caution, particularly in high doses or in combination with other medications.
